A '''magic series''' is a set of distinct positive [[integer]]s which add up to the [[magic constant]] of a [[magic square]] and a [[magic cube]], thus potentially making up lines in [[magic tesseract]]s.

So, in an ''n'' × ''n'' magic square using the numbers from 1 to ''n''<sup>2</sup>, a magic series is a set of ''n'' distinct numbers adding up to ''n''(''n''<sup>2</sup>&nbsp;+&nbsp;1)/2.  For ''n'' = 2, there are just two magic series, 1+4 and 2+3.  The eight magic series when ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;3 all appear in the rows, columns and diagonals of a 3 × 3 magic square.

[[Maurice Kraitchik]] gave the number of magic series up to ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;7 in ''Mathematical Recreations'' in 1942 {{OEIS|id=A052456}}.  In 2002, [[Henry Bottomley]] extended this up to ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;36 and independently [[Walter Trump]] up to ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;32.  In 2005, Trump extended this to ''n''&nbsp;=&nbsp;54 (over 2 × 10<sup>111</sup>) while Bottomley gave an experimental approximation for the numbers of magic series: 
:<math>\frac{1}{\pi} \cdot \sqrt{\frac{3}{e}} \cdot \frac{(e n)^n}{n^3-\frac{3}{5}n^2+\frac{2}{7}n}</math>
In July 2006, [[Robert Gerbicz]] extended this sequence up to ''n''&nbsp;=&thinsp;150.

In 2013 [[Dirk Kinnaes]] was able to exploit his insight that the magic series could be related to the volume of a [[polytope]]. Trump used this new approach to extend the sequence up to ''n''&nbsp;=&thinsp;1000.<ref name = "Trump">Walter Trump http://www.trump.de/magic-squares/</ref>

[[Mike Quist]] showed that the exact second-order count has a multiplicative factor of <math>\tfrac{1}{n^3}\!\left(1+\tfrac{3}{5n}+\tfrac{31}{420n^2}+\cdots\right)</math> equivalent to a  denominator of <math>n^3-\tfrac{3}{5}n^2+\left(\tfrac{2}{7} + \tfrac{1}{2100} \right)\!n+ \cdots.</math><ref name = "Quist">{{Cite arXiv |eprint = 1306.0616|last1 = Quist|first1 = Michael|title = Asymptotic enumeration of magic series|year = 2013|class = math.CO}}</ref>  

[[Richard Schroeppel]] in 1973 published the complete enumeration of the order 5 magic squares at 275,305,224. This recent magic series work gives hope that the relationship between the magic series and the magic square  may provide an exact count for order 6 or order 7 magic squares.  Consider an intermediate structure that lies in complexity between the magic series and the magic square. It might be described as an amalgamation of 4 magic series that have only one unique common integer. This structure forms the two major diagonals and the central row and column for an [[parity (mathematics)|odd]] order magic square. Building blocks such as these could be the way forward.
